{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *ACL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone, while compact exception events achieve near-perfect accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) across all four models, an 18--23pp gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex exploiting a format marker matches this ceiling, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses the regex to near-chance while SFT retains $>$97\%; cross-dataset transfer confirms SFT acquires diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics corroborate this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without convergence (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance transition near 512 tokens, coinciding with the first appearance of structured execution markers (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

While exception events structurally encode verdict direction (exception present typically implies failure), the non-trivial finding is that providing strictly more information (complete traces containing all exception data) degrades performance by 18--23pp.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy} despite containing all diagnostic information: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) remain near source-code-only levels while compact exception events close an 18--23pp gap to ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\item \textbf{Semantic vs.\ format-marker decomposition}: marker removal collapses a format-exploiting regex by 71pp while SFT drops only 2pp; cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows the learned signal generalizes beyond format markers (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{A two-tier signal hierarchy}: exception/assertion signals (${\geq}$98.53\%) dominate loop compression (77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs; a sharp transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

\item \textbf{Mechanistic decomposition}: controlled gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference, though forward-pass attention is an unquantified residual (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}

treat as descriptive), but captures only the \\\\emph{explicit} diagnostic pathway; tail-truncated conditions achieve 93--98\\\\% with $d {\\\\approx} 0$, indicating a second, implicit signal channel operating through terminal execution state (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:density}).\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Dataset}\\n\\\\label{sec:dataset}\\n\\nWe sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\\\\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \\\\citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \\\\citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \\\\texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\\\\% pass, 33\\\\% fail).\\nThe dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\\\\%).\\nThe \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\\\\% train, 48.99\\\\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Trace Representations}\\n\\nWe define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\\\\ref{fig:trace_overview}):\\n\\\\begin{itemize}\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{no\\\\_trace}: Source code and test input only.\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{VOTA} (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction): Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only}: Only exception/error events.\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{ae\\\\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{loop\\\\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.\\n\\\\item \\\\texttt{VOTA\\\\_no\\\\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.\\n\\\\end{itemize}\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure*}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\includegraphics[width=\\\\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}\\n\\\\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace. Four conditions vary the trace information: \\\\texttt{no\\\\_trace} (75.13\\\\%), \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace} (81.44\\\\%), VOTA (99.05\\\\%), and \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} (99.83\\\\%). Accuracies for Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$); multi-seed means where available (Table~\\\\ref{tab:ablation}). Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}\\n\\\\label{fig:trace_overview}\\n\\\\end{figure*}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Models and Training}\\n\\nWe evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \\\\textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \\\\citep{qwen2024coder}, \\\\textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \\\\citep{roziere2024code}, and \\\\textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \\\\citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\\\\times$).\\nAll conditions use LoRA \\\\citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\\\\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, LR $2 \\\\times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.\\nSequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.\\nThe primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} robustness (Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:training_details}).\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Loss Ablation}\\n\\nTo probe the contribution of gradient dilution, we introduce \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace\\\\_label\\\\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).\\nTRL's SFTTrainer computes mean cross-entropy over label tokens, so label-only loss does not amplify the effective learning rate.\\nHowever, this ablation simultaneously changes three variables: (1)~which tokens receive gradient updates, (2)~the implicit regularization from predicting trace tokens, and (3)~the training signal distribution.\\nThe resulting improvement over standard \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace} provides a confounded upper bound on gradient dilution's contribution.\\nA cleaner test (masking 99.8\\\\% of gradient updates during \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} training) matches the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input, isolating gradient dilution from content quality (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:density}).\\n\", \"stderr\": \"\", \"return_code\": 0}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {\"elapsed_seconds\": 0.42}}"}

below 384 tokens, the globals module dump consumes the entire budget, yielding near-\\\\texttt{no\\\\_trace} performance.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Diagnostic signal dilution in complete traces.}\\nBoth pathways' signals exist in full traces but are buried under thousands of intermediate tokens.\\nControlled gradient masking (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:density}) attributes ${\\\\leq}$4\\\\% of the gap to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference: diagnostic tokens are too sparse for the model to reliably extract from verbose input.\\nTraining dynamics (Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) corroborate this: \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} converges within 50 steps while \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace} oscillates without convergence.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Why SFT over regex?}\\nThe contribution is the diagnostic decomposition, not a prediction system; nonetheless, SFT dominates regex on every axis beyond raw accuracy.\\nSFT retains 97.65\\\\% under marker removal while the regex collapses to 28.49\\\\% (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:nomarker}), provides 63$\\\\times$ better calibration (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:calibration}), and transfers bidirectionally across datasets with negligible loss.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Design implications.}\\nComplete traces capture only 3--6pp of the ${\\\\sim}$25pp headroom over source code alone, while exception events capture 23--27pp.\\nThis runs counter to the field's operating assumption that more trace information should help \\\\citep{chen2025tracepile,wang2025dcsh}; below 384 tokens, the globals module dump consumes the entire budget, yielding near-\\\\texttt{no\\\\_trace} performance.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Diagnostic signal dilution in complete traces.}\\nBoth pathways' signals exist in full traces but are buried under thousands of intermediate tokens.\\nControlled gradient masking (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:density}) attributes ${\\\\leq}$4\\\\% of the gap to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference: diagnostic tokens are too sparse for the model to reliably extract from verbose input.\\nTraining dynamics (Appendix~\\\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) corroborate this: \\\\texttt{exception\\\\_only} converges within 50 steps while \\\\texttt{full\\\\_trace} oscillates without convergence.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Why SFT over regex?}\\nThe contribution is the diagnostic decomposition, not a prediction system; nonetheless, SFT dominates regex on every axis beyond raw accuracy.\\nSFT retains 97.65\\\\% under marker removal while the regex collapses to 28.49\\\\% (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:nomarker}), provides 63$\\\\times$ better calibration (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:calibration}), and transfers bidirectionally across datasets with negligible loss.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Design implications.}\\nComplete traces capture only 3--6pp of the ${\\\\sim}$25pp headroom over source code alone, while exception events capture 23--27pp.\\nThis runs counter to the field's operating assumption that more trace information should help \\\\citep{chen2025tracepile,wang2025dcsh}; content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"stdout\": \"\\\\section{Related Work}\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}\\nTracePile \\\\citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \\\\citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility task- and format-dependent, which we extend by showing that complete traces degrade SFT performance while compact exception events suffice.\\nNExT \\\\citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \\\\citep{eguchi2025etcot} used trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning; \\\\citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our density finding.\\nCRUXEval \\\\citep{gu2024cruxeval,xu2025cruxevalx} and LiveCodeBench \\\\citep{jain2024livecodebench} established execution reasoning benchmarks including test output prediction, but none decompose which trace components contribute to \\\\emph{classification} accuracy.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}\\nTRACED \\\\citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; CC2Vec \\\\citep{hoang2020cc2vec}, LLM4PatchCorrect \\\\citep{zhou2024llm4patch}, and APPT \\\\citep{appt2024} developed representation learning of code changes.\\nVerdict prediction is an instance of the test oracle problem \\\\citep{barr2015oracle}.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Fault Localization and Trace Selection.}\\nSBFL \\\\citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar} and LLM-based FL \\\\citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.\\nTraceCoder \\\\citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \\\\citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction; agent-based repair systems \\\\citep{bouzenia2025repairagent,xia2024agentless,yang2024sweagent} incorporate execution feedback, yet which trace components carry verdict signals most efficiently remains unstudied.\\nPrompt compression \\\\citep{jiang2023llmlingua,li2023selectivecontext} showed pruning low-information tokens preserves accuracy; our decomposition quantifies \\\\emph{why}.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Calibration, Data Selection, and Defect Prediction.}\\nNeural network calibration \\\\citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \\\\citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,spiess2025calibration}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; %% ============================================================
\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
\label{sec:vota_examples}

We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.

\paragraph{Fail example.}
A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

## Test Input
divide(1, 0)

## Expected Output
inf

## VOTA Trace
[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

## Verdict
fail
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

\paragraph{Pass example.}
No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

## Test Input
add(2, 3)

## Expected Output
5

## VOTA Trace
[LOOP] No loops detected.
[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5

## Verdict
pass
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, consistent with complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Experiments}

We evaluate across two research questions:
(1)~Why do complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information?
(2)~Which trace components carry the verdict signal, and how does their density affect learning?
All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Problem-level partition (472 train / 119 test, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). \texttt{exception\_only} duplicates (48.99\% test; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}) arise from within-problem variants; deduplication yields negligible ($<$0.1pp) delta.}
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.
Under problem-level clustered bootstrap ($n_\text{eff}{=}119$), all cross-tier gaps remain significant ($p{<}.001$); 3 of 80 within-tier pairwise comparisons lose significance after Holm--Bonferroni correction.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning an 8.7$\times$ parameter range (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families under key conditions; single-seed entries are marked with $^\dag$.
Regex B5 (99.33\%) exploits the \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} format marker, providing a non-learned baseline; its collapse to 28.49\% under marker removal (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}) shows the SFT advantage is not format-driven.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy (\%, $N{=}1{,}190$) across four models (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families. Multi-seed entries report mean$\pm$std over 2--3 seeds; $^\dag$ = single seed (seed 42). Bold: best per model. Full per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}; per-class metrics in Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%

ae\_only & 99.64{\scriptsize$\pm$0.49} & 98.83{\scriptsize$\pm$0.36} & 99.08{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & 98.53{\scriptsize$\pm$0.30} \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & 99.54{\scriptsize$\pm$0.06} & 98.74{\scriptsize$\pm$0.24} & 99.25$^\ddag$ \\

Majority baseline & \multicolumn{4}{c}{71.51} \\
\bottomrule

}
\vspace{2pt}

Per-seed breakdowns for all conditions in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}.

\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Regex baselines illustrate this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, showing it is entirely format-dependent.
The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.

\paragraph{Cross-dataset transfer.}
Bidirectional evaluation demonstrates generalization: HumanEval${\to}$MBPP \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.41\% ($N{=}4{,}270$) and MBPP${\to}$HumanEval achieves 100.0\% ($N{=}1{,}640$), while \texttt{no\_trace} drops to near-majority baseline in both directions (70.56\% vs.\ 69.02\% majority; 67.99\% vs.\ 61.65\%).
The near-zero transfer loss for exception signals, across independently authored problem sets with no problem overlap, shows SFT learns language-level diagnostic patterns, not dataset-specific artifacts.
Under marker removal, cross-dataset accuracy drops to 95.5\% ($-$3.9pp), indicating that the majority of cross-dataset transfer relies on learned diagnostic patterns rather than format markers.

\label{sec:density}

The 18.07pp gap between \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) and \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) could reflect gradient dilution (diagnostic tokens are ${\sim}$1/500 of full traces, diluting gradient signal during training) or content quality (verbose input buries diagnostic signals at inference).

\paragraph{Controlled gradient masking.}
To isolate gradient dilution, we mask 99.8\% of gradient updates during \texttt{exception\_only} training, matching the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input.
This yields 99.22\% (mean $-$0.61pp from \texttt{exception\_only}, 3 seeds), limiting gradient dilution to ${\leq}$4\% of the 18.07pp gap (Table~\ref{tab:density}).
The gradient masking bound attributes the remaining ${\geq}$96\% to content quality (diagnostic signal density at inference), though forward-pass attention during masked training is an unquantified residual.

\section{Cross-Dataset Generalization: DebugBench}

To test whether exception-based verdict prediction generalizes beyond LLM-generated solutions, we evaluate on DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench}, a dataset of human-written programs with synthetically injected bugs (single-point mutations such as operator replacement, variable misuse, and missing statements).

Table~\ref{tab:debugbench} shows that the component ranking from the main experiments is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} (100.00\%) $\geq$ VOTA (99.77\%) $>$ \texttt{no\_trace} (96.71\%).
The \texttt{exception\_only} condition achieves perfect accuracy, showing that the exception-based representation generalizes to a different fault distribution without degradation.

The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.

These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.
